title: Choose the reading world
question: The fresh roll assigned Cassette J-card. Which world feels right for long-form reading and moving across saved articles, research previews, and CVEs?

options.label: Cassette J-card
options.lineage: Hand-ruled cassette inlay cards and liner notes
options.thesis: A folded reading queue keeps the source, order, and the reader’s own notes together.
options.viewport: The open J-card becomes the reader: a quiet left spine names source shelves, a narrow top strip identifies the selected article or CVE, the center holds a generous long-form reading measure, and the folded inner panel carries highlights and notes. Saved sources unfold into a legible, dated queue; no album artwork is invented.
options.risk: The A/B split can feel imposed on articles and CVEs; the two sides must stay optional and never replace topic shelves.

raised.raise: A changed record keeps its identity and its notice until the reader has seen it.
Source type and reading state remain distinct even in compact layouts.
Reading progress has a real, continuous position in the margin.
A source’s own real image may identify it; the interface never fabricates cover art.

options.label: Standards Draft and Errata
options.lineage: Internet standards, revision histories, and errata records
options.thesis: Every source stays readable beside its provenance, section anchors, and changes.
options.viewport: A focused document column with a stable source rail, section anchors, and a slim margin for highlights. An index links articles, research previews, and CVE records by topic.
options.risk: The standards idiom is precise but may make general interest reading feel technical.

options.label: Transit Diagram
options.thesis: Follow topic lines across article, research, and vulnerability shelves without losing your place.
options.viewport: The reader remains a calm, conventional document; a separate topic diagram reveals the available branches and source interchanges, never shrinking the whole network into the reading view.
options.case: Clear fit for moving among mixed sources; lower identification than a personal reading artifact.
options.risk: Topic relationships could be mistaken for literal or curated connections that the app does not provide.

options.label: Split-Flap Status Board
options.thesis: A changed record holds its place and makes its updated state easy to notice.
options.viewport: The reading pane stays settled while a compact register updates source metadata in place; a visible marked state distinguishes a real update from ordinary reading progress.
options.case: Strong state clarity for updates; commuter urgency weakens the calm reading scene.
options.risk: Animated updates would distract from long-form text and depend on update events the app may not have.

options.label: Dense Utility Mosaic
options.thesis: Put many source tools and compact records within one glance.
options.viewport: A dense shelf mosaic collapses into a text-only source index when an article is open.
options.case: Kept: source type and reading state must remain explicit wherever compact metadata appears.
options.risk: The crowded module grid works against calm reading and the user’s stated rejection of dashboard-like density.

options.label: Movement Score
options.thesis: Give continuous reading progress a legible position beside the document.
options.viewport: A slim reading-progress staff sits at the page edge; the article stays in ordinary paragraphs and headings.
options.case: Kept: progress should have a visible, continuous position and remain accessible without animation.
options.risk: Dance notation has little connection to saving and reading research sources.

options.label: Streaming Catalog Wall
options.thesis: Let one selected source take focus while neighboring shelves recede.
options.viewport: A selected reading item opens into a text-first view; neighboring source shelves stay one navigation action away.
options.case: Kept: a real source image can help identify a saved item, but it is always secondary to its title and type.
options.risk: Poster tiles imply a video catalog and push reading into a secondary position.

options.label: Cassette J-card
options.thesis: Keep an ordered list of sources and the reader’s notes together.
options.viewport: A reading queue with a compact source spine and an open document area.
options.case: Kept: identity, order, and personal annotation form a durable reading record.
options.risk: An album side metaphor imposes a sequence that mixed-source shelves do not need.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A conventional reading library, carefully executed and easy to scan.
canonCard.viewport: Familiar navigation to saved articles, discovery, notebook, and CVEs; opening an article expands into a focused reader with notes.
canonCard.risk: The clearest route, but the least distinctive visual identity by design.
